{{distinguish|Multivariate linear regression}}
[[File:Linear least squares2.png|thumb|Quadratic fit as an example of multiple linear regression.]]
{{Regression bar}}

'''Multiple linear regression''', also known as '''multivariable linear regression''',<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hidalgo |first1=Bertha |last2=Goodman |first2=Melody |author-link2=Melody Goodman |date=2012-11-15 |title=Multivariate or Multivariable Regression? |journal=American Journal of Public Health |volume=103 |issue=1 |pages=39–40 |doi=10.2105/AJPH.2012.300897 |issn=0090-0036 |pmc=3518362 |pmid=23153131}}</ref> is a generalization of [[simple linear regression]] to the case of more than one [[independent variable]]. The basic model for multiple linear regression is

:<math> Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \ldots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \epsilon_i</math>

for each observation <math display="inline">i = 1, \ldots , n </math>.

In the formula above we consider ''n'' observations of one dependent variable and ''p'' independent variables. Thus, ''Y''<sub>''i''</sub> is the ''i''<sup>th</sup> observation of the dependent variable, ''X''<sub>''ij''</sub> is ''i''<sup>th</sup> observation of the ''j''<sup>th</sup> independent variable, ''j'' = 1, 2, ..., ''p''. The values ''β''<sub>''j''</sub> represent parameters to be estimated, and ''ε''<sub>''i''</sub> is the ''i''<sup>th</sup> independent identically distributed normal error.

Nearly all real-world regression models involve multiple predictors, and basic descriptions of linear regression are often phrased in terms of the multiple regression model. Note, however, that in these cases the response variable ''y'' is still a scalar.

Multiple linear regression is a [[special case]], restricted to one [[dependent variable]], of [[general linear model]]s (also known as [[multivariate linear regression]]), which predicts multiple [[correlated]] dependent variables.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Rencher |first1=Alvin C. |title=Methods of Multivariate Analysis |volume=709 |page=19 |year=2012 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0g-PAuKub3QC&pg=PA19 |access-date=2015-02-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241004183607/https://books.google.com/books?id=0g-PAuKub3QC&pg=PA19#v=onepage&q&f=false |archive-date=2024-10-04 |url-status=live |series=Wiley Series in Probability and Statistics |chapter=Chapter 10, Multivariate regression – Section 10.1, Introduction |edition=3rd |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-1-118-39167-9 |last2=Christensen |first2=William F.}}.</ref>

==Formulation==
Given a [[data set]] <math>\{y_i,\, x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{ip}\}_{i=1}^n</math> of ''n'' [[statistical unit]]s, a linear regression model assumes that the relationship between the dependent variable <math>y</math> and the vector of regressors <math>\textbf{x}</math> is [[linear function|linear]]. This relationship is modeled through a ''disturbance term'' or ''error variable'' <math>\varepsilon</math> — an unobserved [[random variable]] that adds extra "noise" to the linear relationship between the dependent variable and regressors. Thus the model takes the form<math display="block">y_i = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{p} x_{ip} + \varepsilon_i
 = \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}_i\boldsymbol\beta + \varepsilon_i,
 \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n,</math>where <math>^\mathsf{T}</math> denotes the [[transpose]], so that <math>\mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}_i\boldsymbol{\beta}</math> is the [[inner product]] between [[coordinate vector|vectors]] <math>\mathbf{x}_i</math> and <math>\boldsymbol \beta</math>.

Often these ''n'' equations are stacked together and written in [[matrix notation]] as
: <math>
 \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon, \,
 </math>
where
: <math>
 \mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{bmatrix}, \quad
</math>
: <math>
 \mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}_1 \\ \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}_2 \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}_n \end{bmatrix}
 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 &  x_{11} & \cdots & x_{1p} \\
 1 & x_{21} & \cdots & x_{2p} \\
  \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
 1 & x_{n1} & \cdots & x_{np}
 \end{bmatrix},
</math>
: <math>
 \boldsymbol\beta = \begin{bmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \\ \vdots \\ \beta_p \end{bmatrix}, \quad
 \boldsymbol\varepsilon = \begin{bmatrix} \varepsilon_1 \\ \varepsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\ \varepsilon_n \end{bmatrix}.
 </math>

===Notation and terminology===
* <math>\mathbf{y}</math> is a vector of observed values <math>y_i\ (i=1,\ldots,n)</math> of the variable called the ''regressand'', ''endogenous variable'', ''response variable'', ''target variable'', ''measured variable'', ''criterion variable'', or ''[[dependent variable]]''. This variable is also sometimes known as the ''predicted variable'', but this should not be confused with ''predicted values'', which are denoted <math>\hat{y}</math>. The decision as to which variable in a data set is modeled as the dependent variable and which are modeled as the independent variables may be based on a presumption that the value of one of the variables is caused by, or directly influenced by the other variables. Alternatively, there may be an operational reason to model one of the variables in terms of the others, in which case there need be no presumption of causality.
* <math>\mathbf{X}</math> may be seen as a matrix of [[Row and column vectors|row-vectors]] <math>\mathbf{x}_{i\cdot}</math> or of ''n''-dimensional [[Row and column vectors|column-vectors]] <math>\mathbf{x}_{\cdot j}</math>, which are known as ''regressors'', ''exogenous variables'', ''explanatory variables'', ''covariates'', ''input variables'', ''predictor variables'', or ''[[independent variables]]'' (not to be confused with the concept of [[independent random variables]]). The matrix <math>\mathbf{X}</math> is sometimes called the ''[[design matrix]]''.
** {{anchor|Intercept}}Usually a constant is included as one of the regressors. In particular, <math>x_{i0}=1</math> for <math>i=1,\ldots,n</math>. The corresponding element of '''''β''''' is called the ''[[Y-intercept|intercept]]''. Many statistical inference procedures for linear models require an intercept to be present, so it is often included even if theoretical considerations suggest that its value should be zero.
** Sometimes one of the regressors can be a non-linear function of another regressor or of the data values, as in [[polynomial regression]] and [[segmented regression]]. The model remains linear as long as it is linear in the parameter vector '''''β'''''.
** The values ''x''<sub>''ij''</sub> may be viewed as either observed values of [[random variable]]s ''X''<sub>''j''</sub> or as fixed values chosen prior to observing the dependent variable. Both interpretations may be appropriate in different cases, and they generally lead to the same estimation procedures; however different approaches to [[asymptotic analysis]] are used in these two situations.
* <math>\boldsymbol\beta</math> is a <math>(p+1)</math>-dimensional ''parameter vector'', where <math>\beta_0</math> is the intercept term (if one is included in the model—otherwise <math>\boldsymbol\beta</math> is ''p''-dimensional). Its elements are known as ''effects'' or ''regression coefficients'' (although the latter term is sometimes reserved for the ''estimated'' effects). In [[simple linear regression]], ''p''=1, and the coefficient is known as ''regression slope''{{anchor|Slope}}. Statistical [[estimation theory|estimation]] and [[statistical inference|inference]] in linear regression focuses on '''''β'''''. The elements of this parameter vector are interpreted as the [[partial derivative]]s of the dependent variable with respect to the various independent variables.
* <math>\boldsymbol\varepsilon</math> is a vector of values <math>\varepsilon_i</math>. This part of the model is called the ''error term'', ''disturbance term'', or sometimes ''noise'' (in contrast with the "signal" provided by the rest of the model). This variable captures all other factors which influence the dependent variable ''y'' other than the regressors '''x'''. The relationship between the error term and the regressors, for example their [[correlation]], is a crucial consideration in formulating a linear regression model, as it will determine the appropriate estimation method.

==Solution==
{{further|Linear least squares}}
Fitting a linear model to a given data set usually requires estimating the regression coefficients <math>\boldsymbol\beta</math> such that the error term <math>\boldsymbol\varepsilon=\mathbf{y}- \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta </math> is minimized. For example, it is common to use the sum of squared errors <math>\|\boldsymbol\varepsilon\|_2^2</math> as a measure of <math>\boldsymbol\varepsilon</math> for minimization.

==Example==
Consider a situation where a small ball is being tossed up in the air and then we measure its heights of ascent ''h<sub>i</sub>'' at various moments in time ''t<sub>i</sub>''. Physics tells us that, ignoring the [[Drag (physics)|drag]], the relationship can be modeled as
: <math>
 h_i = \beta_1 t_i + \beta_2 t_i^2 + \varepsilon_i,
 </math>
where ''β''<sub>1</sub> determines the initial velocity of the ball, ''β''<sub>2</sub> is proportional to the [[standard gravity]], and ''ε''<sub>''i''</sub> is due to measurement errors. Linear regression can be used to estimate the values of ''β''<sub>1</sub> and ''β''<sub>2</sub> from the measured data. This model is non-linear in the time variable, but it is linear in the parameters ''β''<sub>1</sub> and ''β''<sub>2</sub>; if we take regressors '''x'''<sub>''i''</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;(''x''<sub>''i''1</sub>, ''x''<sub>''i''2</sub>) &nbsp;=&nbsp;(''t''<sub>''i''</sub>, ''t''<sub>''i''</sub><sup>2</sup>), the model takes on the standard form
: <math>
 h_i = \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}_i\boldsymbol\beta + \varepsilon_i.
 </math>
